idiom_name: lock statement over a dedicated lock object (System.Threading.Lock on .NET 9+)
implementation_notes: The compiler implements the pattern: lock (x) { ... } compiles to Monitor.Enter/Exit inside try/finally - or, when the compiler knows x is a System.Threading.Lock, to a using over Lock.EnterScope() - so a class merely holds a dedicated lock object and publishes it (a lock-typed property) or keeps it private while exposing locked methods. The documented .NET 9/C# 13 guidance is to lock a dedicated System.Threading.Lock instance for best performance, to hold a lock for as short a time as possible, and never to lock this, a Type instance or an interned string because foreign code can reach those objects. System.Threading.ReaderWriterLockSlim and SemaphoreSlim are the library options when mutual exclusion is too coarse or the critical section must be awaited.
pitfalls: lock is reentrant per thread, but Monitor.Exit must run on the thread that entered, await is a compile error inside a lock body, and holding a lock across await deadlocks - use SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync for async critical sections.
Locking on this, typeof(T) or a string literal is documented as unsafe: callers, reflection or the intern table can hold the same lock; use a dedicated private object (or Lock).

A struct cannot be locked (it boxes on demand), and copying a class that advertises its lock while holding mutable state can split the invariants - keep the lock private or the class sealed and immutable outside the lock.
Casting a System.Threading.Lock to object before locking silently falls back to Monitor semantics (the compiler warns about it); publish the concrete Lock type.
